title: Non Clustered Index
description: Understand InnoDB secondary lookups, primary-key locators, composite prefixes, covering queries, and the measured tradeoffs of extra indexes.

questions.question_text: What does a non-clustered index's leaf entry actually contain?
options: The complete row data for every column
The indexed value plus a pointer/reference back to the actual row stored elsewhere
Nothing; it is an empty placeholder
A duplicate of the clustered index
questions.explanation: Unlike a clustered index, a non-clustered index's leaves hold the indexed value and a pointer back to where the full row actually lives.

questions.question_text: How many non-clustered indexes can a single table have?
options: At most one, same as a clustered index
Zero only
Many — there is no 'one per table' restriction like there is for clustered indexes
Exactly the same number as columns in the table, no more no less
questions.explanation: Because non-clustered indexes are separate structures that don't dictate physical row order, a table can have many of them.

questions.question_text: Why does looking up a row via a non-clustered index typically require an extra step compared to a clustered index?
options: It doesn't; both are equally direct
Because the non-clustered index only gives a pointer, requiring a second lookup to fetch the actual row from wherever it's stored
Because non-clustered indexes are always unsorted
Because non-clustered indexes cannot use B+ Trees
questions.explanation: The non-clustered index search yields a pointer, and a second 'bookmark lookup' step is needed to retrieve the actual row.

questions.question_text: What is this extra step (finding the pointer, then fetching the actual row) commonly called?
options: A hash collision
A bookmark lookup (or key lookup)
A table scan
A page split
questions.explanation: This two-step access pattern is commonly referred to as a bookmark or key lookup.

questions.question_text: If `students` is clustered on `id` and has a non-clustered index on `department`, what does the non-clustered index's pointer typically reference?
options: Nothing; it stores full rows directly
The clustered key value (e.g., the id), used to then find the full row via the clustered index
A random row in the table
Another non-clustered index
questions.explanation: On a clustered table, non-clustered index entries typically point via the clustered key, which is then used to locate the actual row.

questions.question_text: Why might a table have non-clustered indexes on department, gpa, AND email simultaneously?
options: Because only one index total is allowed per table
Because each non-clustered index optimizes a different query pattern without affecting the single physical row order
Because non-clustered indexes replace the need for a table entirely
Because SQL requires every column to be indexed
questions.explanation: Multiple non-clustered indexes let different queries each get fast lookups on their respective filter columns, all independent of physical storage order.

questions.question_text: What is a real cost of adding many non-clustered indexes to a table?
options: The table can no longer be read from
Inserts, deletes and updates to relevant indexed keys or stored locators can add maintenance work and write overhead
Non-clustered indexes make the clustered index disappear
Reads become slower with more non-clustered indexes
questions.explanation: Inserts, deletes and changes to indexed keys or stored row locators can require secondary-index maintenance. Updating an unrelated nonindexed column need not rewrite every secondary entry.

questions.question_text: How can the extra 'bookmark lookup' hop of a non-clustered index be avoided for a specific query?
options: It cannot ever be avoided
By using a covering index that includes all columns the query needs, directly in the index itself
By deleting the clustered index
By converting the non-clustered index into a hash index
questions.explanation: A covering index can avoid a clustered lookup for missing row values. InnoDB can still require clustered access forMVCCvisibility under some conditions, so do not promise it never consults the clustered record.

questions.question_text: What does an InnoDB secondary index entry use to locate the full row?
options: The clustered key
A universal raw memory address
The table name only
The SELECT alias
questions.explanation: Secondary entries include the clustered key values.

questions.question_text: What normally organizes InnoDB clustered rows when a primary key is declared?
options: Every secondary index simultaneously
The primary key
The longest text column
The latest query predicate
questions.explanation: The declared primary key normally selects the clustered organization.

questions.question_text: Why does a wide primary key affect secondary index space?
options: It deletes index pages
Its values are carried in secondary entries
Secondary indexes store no keys
It converts indexes into views
questions.explanation: The locator itself contributes storage overhead.

questions.question_text: Which query naturally matches INDEX(member_id, due_date)?
options: Only fee equality with no other predicate
Only an unrelated name suffix
Member equality plus a due date range
Every possible query equally
questions.explanation: The leading member value narrows the date-ordered segment.

questions.question_text: What makes an index covering for a query?
options: It includes every table column always
Its name contains cover
It is always unique
It contains the values required by that query
questions.explanation: Coverage depends on the requested columns and predicates.

questions.question_text: Does a nonunique member index collapse multiple loans for that member?
options: No
Yes, it stores only one loan
Only if fees repeat
Only after SELECT *
questions.explanation: An access path preserves logical rows and their multiplicity.

questions.question_text: Why might a scan be chosen despite an available index on a tiny table?
options: The index necessarily failed to build
Its estimated total cost can be lower
Indexes are never used for integers
Scans change the answer
questions.explanation: Access path choice is cost based.

questions.question_text: What is a cost of adding fee to a covering index?
options: All queries become incorrect
The base fee column disappears
More storage and index maintenance work
Primary keys stop working
questions.explanation: Coverage benefits must justify wider entries and write overhead.

questions.question_text: Does an index change how equality with NULL evaluates?
options: Yes, NULL becomes zero
Yes, NULL matches every value
Only for secondary indexes
No
questions.explanation: Comparison semantics are independent of the access path.

questions.question_text: What is separate from nonunique index navigation?
options: A uniqueness integrity constraint
The table alias
The result header
The SQL comment
questions.explanation: Uniqueness changes permitted data rather than only access paths.

questions.question_text: Which verification supports a claimed performance improvement?
options: The presence of CREATE INDEX text alone
Representative measured workload with correctness checks
A shorter index name
A successful SELECT on three rows
questions.explanation: Plans and measurements substantiate performance claims.

questions.question_text: What is needed before applying a production index change here?
options: Only a screenshot of SQL
A renamed view
Approved migration and operational review
An arbitrary FORCE INDEX hint
questions.explanation: Schema and operational changes follow repository approval rules.

notes:
## A second route to the same rows

A non clustered index provides an access path organized separately from the table's clustered row organization. Terminology differs across engines. In MySQL InnoDB, the relevant structure is usually called a secondary index: the clustered index contains table rows, while secondary entries carry their indexed values and the clustered key needed to locate the corresponding row. This lesson uses that concrete model rather than implying every database stores the same kind of physical pointer.

A campus library stores loans by a primary identifier but frequently looks them up by member and due date. A secondary index can narrow the search without changing the logical loan records. It is a navigation aid, not a second authoritative table maintained by application code. The engine maintains its consistency when indexed values are inserted, updated, or removed.

## Follow an InnoDB lookup

Consider a loans table with primary key id and columns member_id, due_date, and fee. An index on member_id groups relevant entries by that search value. A query asking for all columns for member 7 can locate matching secondary entries and then use their primary keys to retrieve the full clustered rows. This additional lookup matters when many rows qualify.

```sql
CREATE TABLE loans(
 id INT PRIMARY KEY,member_id INT NOT NULL,due_date DATE NOT NULL,fee INT
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
CREATE INDEX ix_loans_member ON loans(member_id);
INSERT INTO loans VALUES
 (10,7,'2026-11-01',4),(11,7,'2026-11-04',6),(12,8,'2026-11-02',8);
SELECT id,member_id,due_date,fee FROM loans
WHERE member_id=7 ORDER BY id;
```

The logical result is loans 10 and 11 regardless of whether the optimizer chooses the index on this tiny fixture. With only three rows, a scan can be cheaper. A correct explanation distinguishes an available access path from a guaranteed chosen plan. Index demonstrations should not invent performance improvements from unmeasured examples.

## Clustered key choice affects every secondary index

InnoDB normally uses the declared primary key as its clustered index. If no primary key exists, it can select an appropriate unique nonnull key; otherwise it creates an internal clustered identifier. Explicitly choosing a short, stable primary key makes row identity and secondary index overhead easier to reason about. It also avoids relying on an implementation fallback as an application identity contract.

Because secondary records include clustered key values, a very wide primary key increases the size of secondary structures. More bytes can mean more pages, more cache pressure, and more maintenance. This does not mean every natural key is wrong; compare integrity, lookup patterns, and storage costs for the actual design. Do not change a production primary key merely to follow a simplistic rule of thumb.

## Composite ordering is intentional

An index on member_id and due_date organizes entries first by member and then by date within each member. It is useful for queries with member equality and a due date range. It can also serve a member only prefix. A due date only query does not have the same straightforward leftmost prefix access, although the optimizer may have other strategies depending on the situation.

```sql
CREATE INDEX ix_loans_member_due ON loans(member_id,due_date);
SELECT id,due_date FROM loans
WHERE member_id=7 AND due_date>='2026-11-01'
ORDER BY due_date,id;
```

This result contains the two member 7 loans in due date order. The index definition follows the query pattern rather than an alphabetical list of columns. A leading range condition can limit how later columns narrow a contiguous search range, though later columns may still help filtering or coverage. Avoid describing the leftmost prefix rule as if later columns become completely useless in every plan.

## Covering queries can avoid some row fetches

A covering index has the values needed by a particular query in the index structure. Coverage is a property of the query and index together, not a permanent label that guarantees every caller is covered. In InnoDB, the primary key carried by a secondary entry can make a query selecting that identifier and indexed columns coverable without repeating the identifier explicitly in the index definition.

A query selecting only id and member_id may be covered by the member index, while selecting fee can require fetching the clustered row. Adding fee to make one report covered enlarges the index and increases write work. Evaluate whether the avoided lookups justify that cost across the complete workload. Do not expand every index to include every table column.

## Duplicate values and uniqueness are separate

A nonunique secondary index can contain many entries for the same member. Each still identifies a different loan through its row key. The index does not collapse those loans, so SELECT without DISTINCT retains all qualifying records. A unique secondary index additionally enforces a uniqueness rule, which changes permitted data and requires a separate integrity decision.

Null values can also appear in appropriate secondary indexes. Ordinary equality with null remains unknown; use IS NULL when the requirement asks for missing values. An index does not change SQL comparison semantics or turn unknown into zero. MySQL's treatment of nullable unique keys also requires attention before using one as a promise that every displayed value identifies exactly one row.

## Worked lab: compare projections

Create the fixture and run EXPLAIN for a query selecting id and member_id for member 7. Then compare a query selecting id, member_id, and fee. Inspect the chosen key and whether the plan indicates coverage. The predicted difference is that fee is absent from the member index, while the primary key and indexed member value are available there. The optimizer may still choose scans on a small table.

To make the exercise useful, populate a safe local fixture with many members and multiple loans each. Keep identical result checks before and after index creation. Record estimated and actual work separately, and do not claim a speedup unless the workload was measured. A warm cache, a tiny table, and repeated execution can make timing comparisons misleading.

## Worked lab: evaluate a compound access path

Compare member equality plus a due date range against a due date only search. Predict why the member and date composite index naturally narrows the first query. Inspect both plans rather than forcing one index to make a demonstration look successful. If the main application instead searches all overdue loans across members, a different leading column may deserve consideration for that workload.

Now update a loan's due_date inside the safe fixture and query it again. The engine must maintain the corresponding composite index entry. This illustrates why extra indexes add write cost even when a particular statement is a read. Inserts, deletes, and updates touching indexed values all contribute to the operational tradeoff; redundant indexes also consume storage and maintenance effort.

## Read plans without turning estimates into facts

An EXPLAIN row estimate describes what the optimizer expects, not an observed count of loans returned to a user. Compare it with the known distribution in the fixture. A member with many loans can require substantial row retrieval even when the index lookup itself is quick. If the application selects nearly every column for nearly every loan, avoiding a table scan may provide little benefit and can add scattered clustered lookups instead.

Likewise, an index that helps one selective member lookup may not be useful for a report over the whole table. Keep both queries in the workload comparison and record which business operation each index is intended to support. This prevents tuning a demonstration while slowing the actual application.

## Review before applying an index change

An index change in a shared production database is an operational and schema change requiring the repository's approval and migration process. Table size, lock behavior, available space, replication, and rollback need review. A lesson's CREATE INDEX snippet is not permission to execute it remotely. Existing application queries and uniqueness constraints must remain compatible with any approved change.

Choose candidate indexes from observed predicates, join keys, ordering, and projection needs. Use statistics and execution plans to decide whether they are chosen, then measure representative read and write workloads. Continue with [Selectivity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/selectivity), [Join Cardinality](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/join-cardinality), and [View Limitations](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/view-limitations) to connect access path choices with row counts and reusable query interfaces.
